title: Stack That Can Pop Its Maximum
statement:
Build a stack that also knows its largest value and can remove it, even when the largest value is buried in the middle.

  • PeakStack() creates an empty stack.
  • push(x) puts x on top.
  • pop() removes the top value and returns it.
  • top() returns the top value without removing it.
  • peekMax() returns the largest value in the stack without removing it.
  • popMax() removes the largest value and returns it. If the largest value appears more than once, remove the copy closest to the top. The other values keep their order.

pop, top, peekMax and popMax are only called on a non-empty stack. Aim for O(log n) per call (amortized is fine); top may be O(1) amortized.

Tests are a list of operations; the first one creates the stack. The output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: popMax pulls the 9 out from under the 2. The stack becomes 4, 2, so the top is still 2 and the new maximum is 4.
There are two 6s. The upper one goes, so 1 is on top afterwards. Removing the bottom 6 would leave a 6 on top.

constraints: pop, top, peekMax and popMax are only called when the stack is not empty
hints: A plain array handles push, pop and top. The hard part is popMax when the maximum is deep inside: you would have to splice it out of the middle.
Keep two views of the same items: a stack in push order and a max-heap by value. Give every pushed item a unique id that grows with time, so ties in the heap can prefer the item closest to the top.
Removing an item from one view leaves a stale copy in the other. Don't hunt for it: record its id as removed, and throw stale entries away only when they reach the top of the stack or the heap.

explain.intuition:
Two questions need two orders. "What is on top?" needs push order, which is a stack. "What is the largest?" needs value order, which is a max-heap. Store every item in both, tagged with an id that grows with each push. In the heap, break ties by the larger id, which is the copy pushed later and so closer to the top.

The problem is that pop removes from the stack but the item still sits somewhere in the heap, and popMax leaves the opposite stale copy. Finding it would be O(n). Instead, use lazy deletion: put the id in a removed set. Before reading the top of either structure, discard entries whose id is in that set. Each item is discarded at most once from each structure, so the cleanup is amortized O(log n) per call. A sorted map plus a doubly linked list is the other classic design. It avoids stale entries, but JavaScript and Python have no built-in sorted map.
steps: Keep stack of [value, id], a max-heap of [value, id] ordered by value then id, a removed set and a counter.
push(x): take a new id, push [x, id] to both.
Cleaning: while the top of the stack (or heap) has an id in removed, discard it and delete the id from the set.
pop() / top(): clean the stack, then pop or read its top. pop adds the id to removed so the heap skips it later.
peekMax() / popMax(): clean the heap, then read or pop its top. popMax adds the id to removed so the stack skips it later.
pitfalls: Breaking heap ties the wrong way. With two equal maxima, popMax must take the newer one (larger id), as the second example shows.
Cleaning only in pop and popMax but not in top and peekMax. A stale top gets reported as a live value.
Using the value as the key in removed. Equal values are different items; only a unique id tells them apart.

solutions.title: Plain array, scan for the maximum
solutions.idea: push, pop and top are array operations. peekMax scans the array, and popMax finds the last index of the maximum and splices it out.
solutions.time: O(n) for peekMax and popMax, O(1) otherwise

solutions.title: Stack + max-heap with lazy deletion
solutions.idea: Both structures hold every item with a unique id. A removal from one marks the id as removed; the other discards it when it reaches the top.

followups: Make every call worst-case O(log n), not amortized. (Hint: a balanced tree keyed by (value, id) plus a doubly linked list.)
If popMax were not needed, how would you get peekMax in O(1) with no heap at all?
